Q: Which exams is Active and Passive Voice useful for?
A: Active and Passive Voice is aligned with the ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC, Railway syllabus. The questions follow the pattern these papers use, so the practice carries over directly to the exam hall.
Q: What is the difference between active and passive voice?
A: In the active voice the subject performs the action, while in the passive voice the subject receives the action.
Q: How is the passive voice formed?
A: The passive is formed with the correct part of the verb "be" plus the past participle of the main verb, keeping the same tense as the active sentence.
Q: Can intransitive verbs be made passive?
A: No. Only transitive verbs, which take an object, can be made passive; intransitive verbs such as sleep and die have no passive form.
Q: How is the passive of an imperative sentence made?
A: With "Let", as in "Open the door" becoming "Let the door be opened", or with "You are requested to".
Q: When is the passive voice used?
A: It is used when the doer is unknown, unimportant or better left unmentioned, and it is common in reports, notices and scientific writing.
Q: Active আৰু passive voice ৰ পাৰ্থক্য কি?
A: Active voice ত কৰ্তাই কামটো কৰে, আনহাতে passive voice ত কৰ্তাই কামটো গ্ৰহণ কৰে।
Q: Passive voice কেনেকৈ গঠন কৰা হয়?
A: "be" ক্ৰিয়াৰ শুদ্ধ ৰূপ আৰু মূল ক্ৰিয়াৰ past participle ৰে passive গঠন কৰা হয়, active বাক্যৰ একে tense ৰাখি।
Q: Intransitive verb ৰ passive কৰিব পাৰিনে?
A: নোৱাৰি। কেৱল object থকা transitive verb ৰ passive কৰিব পাৰি; sleep, die আদি intransitive verb ৰ passive নাই।
Q: Imperative বাক্যৰ passive কেনেকৈ কৰা হয়?
A: "Let" ৰে, যেনে "Open the door" - "Let the door be opened", বা "You are requested to" ৰে।
Q: Passive voice কেতিয়া ব্যৱহাৰ হয়?
A: কৰ্তা অজ্ঞাত, কম গুৰুত্বপূৰ্ণ, বা নকৈ এৰি দিয়াটো ভাল হ'লে ব্যৱহাৰ হয়, আৰু বাতৰি, জাননী আৰু বৈজ্ঞানিক লিখনিত সঘন।

### Articles and Determiners Questions with Answers — ADRE, APSC
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/english/grammar/articles-and-determiners/
Summary: Practice articles and determiners questions with step-by-step answers and explanations for ADRE, APSC and Assam Police. Free, bilingual, no sign-up.
Q: Fill in the blank with the correct article: 'He is ___ honest man.'
A: 'Honest' begins with a silent 'h', so 'an' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ university student.'
A: 'University' begins with the consonant sound /juː/, so 'a' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ M.L.A.'
A: 'M' is pronounced 'em' (a vowel sound), so 'an M.L.A.' is correct.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ Ganges is a holy river.'
A: Names of rivers take 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I saw ___ one-eyed man yesterday.'
A: 'One' is pronounced 'wun' (consonant sound), so 'a' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He plays ___ guitar very well.'
A: Musical instruments take 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'We have ___ dinner at 8 p.m. every day.'
A: Names of meals take no article when used in a general sense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ tallest girl in our class.'
A: Superlative degree always takes 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ taller of the two brothers.'
A: Comparative degree takes 'the' when followed by 'of the two'.
Q: Fill in the blanks: '___ rich should help ___ poor.'
A: 'The + adjective' is used to mean a class of people (the rich = rich people).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ European.'
A: 'European' begins with the sound /jʊə/, a consonant sound, so 'a' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'What ___ lovely dress she is wearing!'
A: Exclamatory 'What a + singular countable noun' pattern is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The Sun rises in ___ east.'
A: Directions (east, west, etc.) after a preposition take 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I met him ___ hour ago.'
A: 'Hour' has a silent 'h', so 'an' is used.
Q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
A: 'Union' begins with the consonant sound /juː/, so 'a' is correct.
Q: Fill in the blank with a suitable article: 'He will arrive in ___ hour.'
A: 'an' (because the 'h' in 'hour' is silent).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Would you like ___ tea?'
A: 'Some' is used in offers and requests even in questions.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I don't have ___ money with me.'
A: 'Any' is used in negative sentences with uncountable nouns.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Did you buy ___ vegetables from the market?'
A: 'Any' is normally used in questions.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'How ___ chairs are there in the hall?'
A: 'Many' is used with countable plural nouns like 'chairs'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'How ___ water is left in the bottle?'
A: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like 'water'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ knowledge is a dangerous thing.'
A: 'A little' means some (positive); here it means some but not enough.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He spent ___ money he had on books.'
A: 'The little' means all that small amount (used when the noun is qualified).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He has ___ friends, so he always feels lonely.'
A: 'Few' means hardly any (negative); the result 'lonely' shows a negative idea.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She has ___ friends who always help her.'
A: 'A few' means some (positive); she has some helpful friends.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ of the boys was given a prize.'
A: 'Every' cannot be followed by 'of'; 'each of' is used with a plural noun.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'You may take ___ of the two books.'
A: 'Either' means any one of the two.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ of the two brothers is honest.'
A: 'Neither' means not one of the two; 'none' is used for more than two.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ the two sisters are teachers.'
A: 'Both' is used for two persons or things together.
Q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
A: 'Information' is an uncountable noun, so 'much' is correct.
Q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
A: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Many a soldier ___ died in the battle.'
A: 'Many a + singular noun' takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The number of tigers in the park ___ decreasing.'
A: 'The number of' is followed by a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank with a suitable determiner: 'He did not have ___ money to lend me.'
A: 'any' (used in negative sentences before uncountable nouns).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He wants to become ___ engineer.'
A: 'Engineer' starts with a vowel sound /e/, so 'an' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I bought ___ umbrella from the shop.'
A: 'Umbrella' begins with a vowel sound, so 'an' is used.
Q: Fill in the blanks: '___ earth moves round ___ sun.'
A: Unique things (the earth, the sun, the moon) take 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ whole is greater than its parts.'
A: 'The whole' is a fixed expression meaning the complete thing.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ Himalayas are in the north of India.'
A: Names of mountain ranges take 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Mount Everest is ___ highest peak in the world.'
A: Superlatives always take 'the'; single mountains like Mount Everest take no article.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She reads ___ Times of India every day.'
A: Names of newspapers and journals take 'the'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'My father goes to the office by ___ bus.'
A: No article is used after 'by' with means of transport (by bus, by train, by air).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He goes to ___ bed at 10 p.m.'
A: In phrases like 'go to bed', 'go to school', 'at home' no article is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The thief was sent to ___ prison.'
A: 'Sent to prison' (as a punishment) takes no article; 'the prison' would mean the building.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The boys play ___ football in the evening.'
A: Names of games and sports take no article.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He speaks ___ English very well.'
A: Names of languages take no article.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'It is such ___ interesting story that everybody likes it.'
A: 'Such a/an + noun' pattern is used; 'interesting' starts with a vowel sound.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ most intelligent boy in the class.'
A: 'The most' is used before the superlative degree.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ only child of her parents.'
A: 'Only' takes 'the' ('the only child').
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This is ___ same pen that I lost.'
A: 'Same' always takes 'the' (the same).
Q: Fill in the blanks: '___ more we get, ___ more we want.'
A: In the 'the + comparative...the + comparative' structure 'the' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ honour to his family.'
A: 'Honour' has a silent 'h', so 'an' is used.
Q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
A: Rivers take 'the', and 'river' being countable needs 'a' here.
Q: Fill in the blank with a suitable article: 'He is ___ heir to the throne.'
A: 'an' (the 'h' in 'heir' is silent).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'There are ___ boys in our class than in yours.'
A: 'Fewer' is used for countable plural nouns (boys).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'There is ___ sugar in this cup than in that one.'
A: 'Less' is used for uncountable nouns (sugar).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'A number of students ___ passed the examination.'
A: 'A number of' takes a plural verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She doesn't like ___ of these dresses.'
A: 'Any' is used in negative sentences.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Is there ___ milk in the fridge?'
A: 'Any' is normally used in questions.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Don't worry; we have ___ time to finish the work.'
A: 'Plenty of' is used with both countable and uncountable nouns.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the girls ___ given a certificate.'
A: 'Each of' takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This is one of the best ___ I have ever read.'
A: After 'one of the + superlative', a plural noun is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Give me ___ milk, please.'
A: Uncountable nouns need a partitive expression like 'a glass of'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ fifty people attended the meeting.'
A: 'Some' before a number means 'about/approximately'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He will come back in ___ days.'
A: 'A few' means some days (positive); he will return.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He takes very ___ interest in his studies.'
A: 'Little' (without article) has a negative sense; 'very little' means hardly any.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'How ___ luggage do you have with you?'
A: 'Luggage' is uncountable, so 'much' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ are my friends from Guwahati.'
A: Demonstrative 'these' is used with the plural noun 'friends'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This pen is not good. Give me ___ one.'
A: 'Another' means one more of the same kind (an + other).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I have two shirts; one is white and ___ is blue.'
A: 'The other' refers to the second of two.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ of the students could answer the question.'
A: 'None of' is used before a noun/pronoun; 'no' is an adjective used directly before a noun.
Q: Fill in the blank with a suitable article: 'He is ___ honourable man.'
A: 'an' (the 'h' in 'honourable' is silent).
Q: Is Articles & Determiners free to use on axomexam?
A: There is no payment involved in Articles & Determiners. The complete set of 25 questions and its step-by-step explanations are open to every visitor, so you can practise without creating an account or paying a fee.
Q: Are the Articles & Determiners questions available in Assamese and English?
A: Yes — the content is fully bilingual. You can switch between Assamese and English at any point while working through Articles & Determiners, which helps when a term is clearer in one language than the other.
Q: Which exams is Articles & Determiners useful for?
A: Articles & Determiners is aligned with the ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC, Railway syllabus. The questions follow the pattern these papers use, so the practice carries over directly to the exam hall.
Q: What is the difference between an article and a determiner?
A: Articles are a, an and the, while determiners are a wider group that includes articles as well as this, some, each, my and many, all of which come before a noun and limit it.
Q: When do we use "a" and when "an"?
A: "A" is used before a consonant sound and "an" before a vowel sound, decided by sound and not spelling, as in "a university" and "an hour".
Q: What is the difference between "few" and "a few"?
A: "Few" means hardly any and has a negative sense, while "a few" means some and has a positive sense; the article changes the meaning.
Q: When is no article used before a noun?
A: No article is used before proper nouns, general plural nouns, abstract nouns used generally, and the names of meals, games, languages and most diseases.
Q: Why are articles and determiners important for competitive exams?
A: They are tested in fill in the blanks, error spotting and cloze tests, and they also decide subject-verb agreement, so they carry marks in every English paper.
Q: Article আৰু determiner ৰ পাৰ্থক্য কি?
A: Article হৈছে a, an, the; আনহাতে determiner এটা ডাঙৰ গোট য'ত article ৰ লগতে this, some, each, my, many আদি থাকে, আৰু এইবোৰ noun-ৰ আগত আহি তাৰ পৰিসৰ নিৰ্ধাৰণ কৰে।
Q: "a" আৰু "an" কেতিয়া ব্যৱহাৰ কৰা হয়?
A: ব্যঞ্জনধ্বনিৰ আগত "a" আৰু স্বৰধ্বনিৰ আগত "an", ধ্বনিৰ ভিত্তিত বানানৰ নহয়, যেনে "a university" আৰু "an hour"।
Q: "few" আৰু "a few" ৰ পাৰ্থক্য কি?
A: "few" মানে প্ৰায় নাই আৰু নঞৰ্থক ভাৱ, আনহাতে "a few" মানে অলপ আৰু ধনাত্মক ভাৱ; article-এ অৰ্থ সলনি কৰে।
Q: কেতিয়া noun-ৰ আগত article নালাগে?
A: Proper noun, সাধাৰণ বহুবচন noun, সাধাৰণ অৰ্থত abstract noun, আৰু ভোজন, খেল, ভাষা আৰু বেছিভাগ ৰোগৰ নামৰ আগত article নালাগে।
Q: প্ৰতিযোগিতামূলক পৰীক্ষাৰ বাবে article আৰু determiner কিয় গুৰুত্বপূৰ্ণ?
A: ইহঁত fill in the blanks, error spotting আৰু cloze test ত সোধা হয়, লগতে subject-verb agreement-ও নিৰ্ণয় কৰে, সেয়ে প্ৰতিটো ইংৰাজী পত্ৰতে নম্বৰ বহন কৰে।

### Direct and Indirect Speech — ADRE, APSC
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/english/grammar/direct-indirect-speech/
Summary: Practice direct and indirect speech questions with step-by-step answers and explanations for ADRE, APSC and Assam Police. Free, bilingual, no sign-up.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I am busy.'
A: Simple present 'am' changes to simple past 'was', and 'I' changes to 'he'.
Q: Choose the correct reporting verb: 'He ___ me that he was tired.'
A: With an object ('me') we use 'told', not 'said'. 'Said to' becomes 'told'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'We are going now.'
A: 'We' changes to 'they', 'are going' to 'were going', and 'now' to 'then'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'The earth moves round the sun.'
A: Universal truths and scientific facts do not change their tense in indirect speech.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'I will help you.'
A: 'Said to' becomes 'told', 'will' becomes 'would', 'I'→'he' and 'you'→'me'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I have finished my work.'
A: Present perfect 'have finished' becomes past perfect 'had finished'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I went to the market yesterday.'
A: Simple past 'went' becomes past perfect 'had gone'; 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day/the day before'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I will come tomorrow.'
A: 'Will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I am reading a novel.'
A: Present continuous 'am reading' becomes past continuous 'was reading'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: They said, 'We have been living here for ten years.'
A: Present perfect continuous becomes past perfect continuous, and 'here' becomes 'there'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I can swim.'
A: 'Can' changes to 'could' in indirect speech.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I may come to the party.'
A: 'May' changes to 'might' in indirect speech.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I shall help you.'
A: 'Shall' (future with I/we) becomes 'would' after a past reporting verb.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I must go now.'
A: In indirect speech 'must' often becomes 'had to'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Open the door.'
A: An imperative becomes 'told + object + to + verb' in indirect speech.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Do not make a noise.'
A: Negative commands take 'told + object + not + to + verb'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Please help me.'
A: A request with 'please' becomes 'requested + object + to + verb'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said, 'Boys, work hard.'
A: An advice-like command becomes 'advised + object + to + verb'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'What are you doing?'
A: Wh-questions keep the question word; the sentence becomes statement order with the tense changed.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Are you ill?'
A: Yes/no questions use 'if/whether' and statement order.
Q: Choose the correct sentence:
A: 'Said' has no object here, and 'will' changes to 'would'. 'Told' needs an object.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He says, 'I am fine.'
A: When the reporting verb is in the present tense ('says'), the tense of the speech does not change.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I was writing a letter.'
A: Past continuous 'was writing' becomes past perfect continuous 'had been writing'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: The boy said, 'Hurrah! We have won the match.'
A: 'Hurrah!' (joy) becomes 'exclaimed with joy that...'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'Alas! I have lost my purse.'
A: 'Alas!' (sorrow) becomes 'exclaimed with sorrow that...'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, 'Where do you live?'
A: The question becomes a statement: 'where I lived' (no 'do').
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Did you see the movie?'
A: Past simple question becomes past perfect: 'if I had seen'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said to me, 'Why were you late?'
A: 'Were' becomes 'had been' and the word order becomes statement order.
Q: Change into indirect speech: Ram said, 'I go to school by bus.'
A: Simple present 'go' becomes simple past 'went' in indirect speech.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I have never seen such a beautiful place.'
A: Present perfect 'have never seen' becomes past perfect 'had never seen'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, 'When will you return?'
A: 'Will' becomes 'would', and the word order becomes statement order.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, 'Do you like tea?'
A: The 'do' is dropped and the tense changes to past: 'if I liked tea'.
Q: Choose the correct reporting verb change: 'Said to' in a statement becomes ___
A: In a plain statement, 'said to' becomes 'told' when an object follows.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, 'I met your brother.'
A: 'I'→'he', 'your'→'her', and 'met'→'had met' (past perfect).
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'This is my book.'
A: 'This' becomes 'that', 'my' becomes 'her', and 'is' becomes 'was'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: They said, 'These flowers are fresh.'
A: 'These' becomes 'those' and 'are' becomes 'were'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I was ill yesterday.'
A: 'Was' becomes 'had been' and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said to us, 'Sit down.'
A: An imperative becomes 'told + object + to + infinitive'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'Let me go home.'
A: 'Let me' (a wish/suggestion) is reported with 'proposed/expressed a wish that...'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'Let us play cricket.'
A: 'Let us' (suggestion) becomes 'proposed/suggested that we should...'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'What a clever boy you are!'
A: Exclamations with 'what/how' become 'exclaimed that...' and 'very' replaces the exclamation.
Q: Which of these is NOT a correct change of time expression?
A: 'Today' becomes 'that day', not 'the next day' (which is for 'tomorrow').
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Have you finished your homework?'
A: Present perfect question becomes past perfect with 'if': 'if I had finished'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I do not like mangoes.'
A: 'Do not like' (simple present) becomes 'did not like' (simple past).
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'I am your friend.'
A: 'I'→'he' (speaker), 'your'→'my' (listener), 'am'→'was' (tense backshift).
Q: Change into indirect speech: The old man said, 'May you live long!'
A: A blessing ('may you') becomes 'prayed that + subject + might + verb'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'Goodbye, my friends!'
A: Parting words 'Goodbye' become 'bade + object + goodbye'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Thank you for your help.'
A: 'Thank you' becomes 'thanked + object', and 'your' changes to 'my'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: Mother said to me, 'Never tell a lie.'
A: A negative advice becomes 'advised + object + never to + verb'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I saw the Taj Mahal last year.'
A: 'Saw' becomes 'had seen' and 'last year' becomes 'the previous year'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said to him, 'Who are you?'
A: 'Who' question keeps the question word but takes statement order: 'who he was'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I came here yesterday.'
A: 'Came'→'had come', 'here'→'there', and 'yesterday'→'the previous day'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'The sun sets in the west.'
A: A universal truth does not change its tense in indirect speech.
Q: Choose the correct indirect speech: He said, 'I would like a cup of tea.'
A: 'Would' does not change after a past reporting verb.
Q: Change into indirect speech: The doctor said to me, 'Take this medicine twice a day.'
A: 'This' becomes 'that' and the imperative becomes 'advised + me + to + take'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Did you eat your lunch?'
A: 'Did you eat' (simple past question) becomes 'if I had eaten' (past perfect).
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I have bought a new sari.'
A: 'Have bought' (present perfect) becomes 'had bought' (past perfect).
Q: In indirect speech, a 'yes/no' question is introduced with which word(s)?
A: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' or 'whether'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'How beautiful the sky is!'
A: Exclamations with 'how' become 'exclaimed that...' with 'very'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, 'Please do not disturb me.'
A: A polite negative request becomes 'requested + me + not + to + disturb'.
Q: Choose the correct change: 'said to me' in a question becomes ___
A: Interrogative sentences are reported with 'ask/enquire/inquire'.
Q: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, 'Whose book is this?'
A: 'This'→'that', 'is'→'was', and the order becomes statement order.
Q: What is narration in English grammar?
A: Narration is the way of reporting a speaker's words, either in the speaker's own words (direct speech) or in our own words (indirect speech).
Q: What changes when direct speech becomes indirect speech?
A: The comma and inverted commas are removed, the reporting verb, pronouns, tense and words of time and place change, and a suitable conjunction such as "that", "if" or "to" is added.
Q: When does the tense not change in narration?
A: The tense does not change when the reporting verb is in the present or future tense, or when the reported speech states a universal truth, a habitual fact or a proverb.
Q: How do questions change in indirect speech?
A: Yes or no questions take "if" or "whether" and statement order, while wh-questions keep the question word but also use statement order.
Q: How are imperatives changed into indirect speech?
A: The reporting verb changes to ordered, told, requested or advised, and the command verb is joined with "to", as in "Close the door" becoming "He told me to close the door".
Q: ইংৰাজী ব্যাকৰণত narration কাক বোলে?
A: Narration হৈছে বক্তাৰ কথা ৰিপ'ৰ্ট কৰাৰ ধৰণ — হয় বক্তাৰ নিজৰ শব্দত (direct speech), নাইবা নিজৰ ভাষাত (indirect speech)।
Q: Direct speech ৰ পৰা indirect speech লৈ যাওঁতে কি কি সলনি হয়?
A: Comma আৰু inverted comma আতৰোৱা হয়, reporting verb, pronoun, tense আৰু সময়-স্থান শব্দ সলনি হয়, আৰু "that", "if" বা "to" ধৰণৰ উপযুক্ত conjunction যোগ কৰা হয়।
Q: Narration ত কেতিয়া tense সলনি নহয়?
A: Reporting verb বৰ্তমান বা ভৱিষ্যত কালত থাকিলে, নাইবা reported speech এ চিৰন্তন সত্য, অভ্যাসগত সত্য বা প্ৰবচন ক'লে tense সলনি নহয়।
Q: Indirect speech ত প্ৰশ্ন কেনেকৈ সলনি হয়?
A: Yes/no প্ৰশ্নই "if" বা "whether" আৰু statement ৰ ক্ৰম লয়, আনহাতে wh-প্ৰশ্নই প্ৰশ্নবোধক শব্দ ৰাখিও statement ৰ ক্ৰম ব্যৱহাৰ কৰে।
Q: Imperative বাক্য indirect speech লৈ কেনেকৈ সলনি হয়?
A: Reporting verb ordered, told, requested বা advised হয়, আৰু ক্ৰিয়াৰ লগত "to" যোগ হয়, যেনে "Close the door" → "He told me to close the door"।

### Subject Verb Agreement Questions with Answers — ADRE, APSC
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/english/grammar/subject-verb-agreement/
Summary: Practice subject verb agreement questions with step-by-step answers and explanations for ADRE, APSC and Assam Police. Free, bilingual, no sign-up.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The news ___ (be) good.'
A: 'News' looks plural but is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Mathematics ___ (be) my favourite subject.'
A: Names of subjects ending in '-s' like mathematics, physics are singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The police ___ (have) caught the thief.'
A: 'Police' is always treated as plural, so the verb is 'have'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the boys ___ (be) given a prize.'
A: 'Each' is singular, so even with 'of the boys' the verb is singular 'was'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Neither of the answers ___ (be) correct.'
A: 'Neither' (one of two) is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Both of them ___ (be) present in the meeting.'
A: 'Both' always takes a plural verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The number of students ___ (be) increasing day by day.'
A: 'The number of' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'A number of students ___ (be) absent today.'
A: 'A number of' is plural, so the verb is 'are'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'One of my friends ___ (be) a doctor.'
A: 'One of + plural noun' takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The quality of these products ___ (be) very good.'
A: The verb agrees with the main subject 'quality', not with 'products'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The Arabian Nights ___ (be) an interesting book.'
A: The title of a book, though plural in form, is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The scissors ___ (be) not in the drawer.'
A: Tools like scissors, trousers, spectacles have two parts and take plural verbs.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Measles ___ (be) a contagious disease.'
A: Diseases like measles, mumps, though ending in 's', are singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The committee ___ (have) submitted its report.'
A: A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The cattle ___ (be) grazing in the field.'
A: 'Cattle' is always plural and takes a plural verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Everyone ___ (have) to attend the meeting.'
A: 'Everyone, everybody, someone' are singular and take singular verbs.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'All the furniture ___ (be) new.'
A: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'There ___ (be) many mangoes in the basket.'
A: In 'there is/are' sentences the verb agrees with the noun that follows.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'There ___ (be) a book and two pens on the table.'
A: The verb agrees with the first or nearest subject: 'a book' is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He as well as his friends ___ (be) guilty.'
A: Words like 'as well as, with, together with' do not change the number; the verb agrees with the first subject 'he'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The teacher along with the students ___ (be) present.'
A: 'Along with' does not affect agreement; the verb agrees with 'the teacher'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'No news ___ (be) good news.'
A: 'News' is singular even with 'no'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The wages of sin ___ (be) death.'
A: The proverb treats 'wages' as a singular amount: 'The wages of sin is death.'
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The poet and philosopher ___ (be) dead.' (one person)
A: When two roles belong to one person (single article 'the'), the verb is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The poet and the philosopher ___ (be) dead.' (two persons)
A: Two separate persons with separate articles 'the ... and the ...' take a plural verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Slow and steady ___ (win) the race.'
A: In this proverb the two adjectives together mean one idea, so the verb is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Bread and butter ___ (be) his daily food.'
A: 'Bread and butter' is one item (food), so it takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Time and tide ___ (wait) for no man.'
A: This proverb always uses the plural verb 'wait'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Either you or he ___ (be) to blame.'
A: With 'either...or / neither...nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here 'he' (is).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Neither he nor I ___ (be) wrong.'
A: The nearer subject is 'I', so the verb is 'am'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Not only he but also his friends ___ (be) invited.'
A: The nearer subject 'his friends' is plural, so the verb is 'were'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Many a man ___ (have) died in the war.'
A: 'Many a + singular noun' takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'More than one person ___ (be) killed in the accident.'
A: Traditionally 'more than one + singular noun' takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Two and two ___ (make) four.'
A: In arithmetic, the verb usually agrees with the nearest number, so 'make' is accepted.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Five thousand rupees ___ (be) a big amount.'
A: A sum of money is treated as one amount, so the verb is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Twenty kilometres ___ (be) a long distance to walk.'
A: A distance is treated as one measure, so the verb is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The United States ___ (be) a big country.'
A: Names of countries like 'The United States' are singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'His spectacles ___ (be) new.'
A: 'Spectacles' has two parts, so it is plural.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The poor ___ (be) helped by the government.'
A: 'The + adjective' (the poor, the rich) refers to many people and is plural.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The old ___ (be) respected in our society.'
A: 'The old' means old people (plural).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'A pair of shoes ___ (be) missing.'
A: The subject is 'a pair', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Physics ___ (be) not easy to learn.'
A: The subject 'Physics' (singular subject name) takes a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Every boy and every girl ___ (wear) a uniform.'
A: Subjects joined by 'and' but each beginning with 'every/each' are singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Either of the two roads ___ (lead) to the station.'
A: 'Either of + plural noun' is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'None but the brave ___ (deserve) the fair.'
A: 'None but' means 'only', and 'the brave' is plural, so the verb is 'deserve'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is one of the best boys that ___ (be) in the class.'
A: In 'one of + plural noun + that', the relative 'that' refers to the plural noun, so the verb is plural.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the girls ___ (have) her own book.'
A: 'Each of' is always singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The jury ___ (be) divided in their opinions.'
A: When the members of a collective noun act separately, we use a plural verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The jury ___ (have) announced its verdict.'
A: When a collective noun acts as one body, we use a singular verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Fifty miles ___ (be) a long way to walk.'
A: A distance is treated as a single measure, so singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The cost of all these articles ___ (have) risen.'
A: The main subject is 'cost' (singular), not 'articles'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Half of the apples ___ (be) rotten.'
A: After 'half of', the verb agrees with the noun: 'apples' is plural.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Half of the cake ___ (be) eaten.'
A: 'Cake' here is uncountable, so the verb is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'A large number of people ___ (be) present at the meeting.'
A: 'A number of' is plural, so 'were' is correct.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The majority of the students ___ (be) hardworking.'
A: 'The majority of + plural noun' usually takes a plural verb.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'To read novels ___ (be) a good habit.'
A: An infinitive phrase used as the subject is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'What he says ___ (be) not true.'
A: A noun clause as the subject is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The leader with his followers ___ (have) arrived.'
A: 'With' does not add to the subject; the verb agrees with 'the leader'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'No one ___ (be) allowed to enter the room.'
A: 'No one' is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Everyone ___ (have) done his duty.'
A: 'Everyone' is singular, so 'has' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The students, not the teacher, ___ (be) responsible for this.'
A: The subject 'the students' is plural; 'not the teacher' is an appositive addition.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Every one of the students ___ (be) present today.'
A: 'Every one of' is singular.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The Himalayas ___ (be) the highest mountains in the world.'
A: Mountain ranges like 'the Himalayas' are plural.

Q: What is subject-verb agreement?
A: Subject-verb agreement is the rule that a verb must match its subject in number and person: a singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb.
Q: Does a phrase between the subject and verb change the verb?
A: No. Words joined by with, along with, as well as, besides and including do not change the number of the verb.
Q: What verb is used after "each" and "everyone"?
A: A singular verb, because each, everyone, everybody, somebody and neither are grammatically singular.
Q: Which verb is used after "neither ... nor"?
A: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, as in "Neither the teacher nor the students were present".
Q: Why do news, mathematics and physics take a singular verb?
A: They are singular in meaning even though they end in -s, so they take a singular verb, as in "The news is good".
Q: Subject-verb agreement কাক বোলে?
A: Subject-verb agreement হৈছে এনে নিয়ম যে ক্ৰিয়াক কৰ্তাৰ সংখ্যা আৰু পুৰুষৰ লগত মিল থাকিব লাগে: একবচন কৰ্তাই একবচন ক্ৰিয়া আৰু বহুবচন কৰ্তাই বহুবচন ক্ৰিয়া লয়।
Q: কৰ্তা আৰু ক্ৰিয়াৰ মাজৰ পদে ক্ৰিয়া সলনি কৰেনে?
A: নকৰে। with, along with, as well as, besides, including ৰে জোৰা লগা শব্দই ক্ৰিয়াৰ সংখ্যা সলনি নকৰে।
Q: "each" আৰু "everyone" ৰ পিছত কোন ক্ৰিয়া আহে?
A: একবচন ক্ৰিয়া, কাৰণ each, everyone, everybody, somebody আৰু neither ব্যাকৰণমতে একবচন।
Q: "neither ... nor" ৰ পিছত কোন ক্ৰিয়া আহে?
A: ক্ৰিয়া ওচৰৰ কৰ্তাৰ লগত মিলে, যেনে "Neither the teacher nor the students were present"।
Q: news, mathematics, physics এ কিয় একবচন ক্ৰিয়া লয়?
A: -s ৰে শেষ হ'লেও ইহঁত অৰ্থত একবচন, সেয়ে একবচন ক্ৰিয়া লয়, যেনে "The news is good"।

### Tenses Questions with Answers — ADRE, APSC
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/english/grammar/tenses/
Summary: Practice tenses questions with step-by-step answers and explanations for ADRE, APSC and Assam Police. Free, bilingual, no sign-up.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She ___ to school every day.'
A: 'Every day' shows a habit, so we use the simple present. With 'she' we add 's/es'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The sun ___ in the east.'
A: A universal truth is always in the simple present tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Look! It ___ (rain) now.'
A: An action happening now uses the present continuous (is + ing).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She ___ (cook) dinner at present.'
A: 'At present' indicates an action going on now, so present continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (finish) my homework just now.'
A: 'Just' suggests a recently completed action, so we use the present perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ (live) here since 2005.'
A: 'Since + a point of time' with an action still continuing takes the present perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'They ___ (play) cricket for two hours.'
A: 'For + a period' with an action started in the past and still going on takes the present perfect continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (visit) my uncle last week.'
A: 'Last week' is a finished past time, so we use the simple past.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The baby ___ (cry) when I came in.'
A: An action going on when another past action happened uses the past continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The train ___ (leave) before we reached the station.'
A: An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ (work) for three hours before the boss came.'
A: An action continuing up to a past point uses the past perfect continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (call) you tomorrow.'
A: 'Tomorrow' indicates a future action, so we use 'will + verb'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She ___ (finish) the work by evening.'
A: 'By + a future time' showing completion takes the future perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This time next week I ___ (travel) to Delhi.'
A: An action in progress at a certain future time uses the future continuous.
Q: 'Since morning' is a marker mainly used with which tense?
A: 'Since + a starting point' is typical of the present perfect / present perfect continuous tense.
Q: 'Yesterday' is a marker mainly used with which tense?
A: 'Yesterday' points to a finished past time, so the simple past is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I met him two days ___.'
A: 'Ago' is used with a past time and the simple past tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She has been working here ___ 2019.'
A: A point of time (2019) takes 'since' in the present perfect.
Q: Which verb does not take the continuous form?
A: 'Know' is a stative verb (state, not action), so we say 'I know', not 'I am knowing'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ (know) the answer to this question.'
A: Stative verbs like 'know' are not used in the continuous form.
Q: 'Every day' is a marker mainly used with which tense?
A: 'Every day' shows a routine, so the simple present tense is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The earth ___ round the sun.'
A: Scientific truths are expressed in the simple present tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (see) him yesterday.'
A: 'Yesterday' takes the simple past. The past of 'see' is 'saw'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She ___ (not, go) to Guwahati last month.'
A: The negative of the simple past is made with 'did not + base verb'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ you ___ (eat) your breakfast yet?'
A: 'Yet' is used with the present perfect: 'Have + past participle'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ (read) a book when the lights went out.'
A: An action in progress in the past when another action interrupted it uses the past continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'When I reached the hall, he ___ (already, leave).'
A: An action that happened before another past action is in the past perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'By next year I ___ (graduate).'
A: 'By + future time' takes the future perfect tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'They ___ (build) this bridge in 1990.'
A: 'In 1990' is a finished past time, so we use the simple past 'built'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The movie ___ (start) before we reached the hall.'
A: The earlier of two past actions is in the past perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (write) this letter since morning.'
A: 'Since morning' with an action still going on takes the present perfect continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'It ___ (not, rain) now.'
A: The negative of the present continuous is 'is/am/are + not + ing'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'How long ___ you ___ (learn) English?'
A: 'How long' asks about duration up to now, so the present perfect continuous is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'My brother ___ (play) cricket every evening.'
A: A routine with a third-person subject takes 'plays' (adds s/es).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She ___ (wash) her clothes at present.'
A: 'At present' shows an action happening now, so present continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The train ___ at 6 pm every day.'
A: Fixed timetables and schedules are expressed in the simple present.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'They ___ (not, watch) TV last night.'
A: 'Last night' takes the simple past negative: 'did not + watch'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'We ___ (live) in Assam for ten years now.'
A: 'For + period + now' shows an action continuing to the present, so the present perfect is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Look! The boy ___ (drown)!'
A: 'Look!' points to an action happening at this moment, so present continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (hear) a strange noise just now.'
A: 'Just now' means a moment ago, so the simple past 'heard' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius.'
A: A scientific fact is in the simple present tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ (sleep) when the phone rang.'
A: An action in progress in the past when interrupted uses the past continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She has been ill ___ Monday.'
A: A point of time (Monday) takes 'since' in the present perfect.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'By the time we arrived, they ___ (eat) everything.'
A: 'By the time + past' requires the past perfect for the earlier action.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This time tomorrow, I ___ (fly) over the clouds.'
A: 'This time tomorrow' shows an action in progress at a future time, so the future continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ you ever ___ (see) the Taj Mahal?'
A: 'Ever' is used with the present perfect: 'Have + past participle'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'They ___ (build) the road for several months.'
A: 'For + period' with an unfinished ongoing action takes the present perfect continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I will call you as soon as I ___ (reach) home.'
A: After 'as soon as / when / if' in a future sentence we use the present tense, not 'will'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, we will cancel the match.'
A: In the first conditional, the 'if' clause takes the simple present and the main clause takes 'will'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The earth ___ (be) round.'
A: A universal truth always stays in the simple present.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He speaks as if he ___ everything.'
A: After 'as if / as though' we use a past tense for an unreal or imaginary comparison.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I wish I ___ (be) a bird.'
A: After 'wish' we use the subjunctive past 'were' for unreal wishes.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'It is high time we ___ (go) home.'
A: After 'It is time / high time' we use a past tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She talks as though she ___ (know) all the answers.'
A: After 'as though / as if' we use the past tense for an unreal situation.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ (go) to Guwahati next month.'
A: 'Next month' is future time, so 'will + go' is used.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ she ___ (like) black tea?'
A: The interrogative of the simple present with 'she' uses 'Does + base verb'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'They ___ (not, come) back yet.'
A: 'Yet' takes the present perfect negative: 'have not + past participle'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The children ___ (play) in the park since 4 o'clock.'
A: 'Since + point of time' with a continuing action takes the present perfect continuous.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ (not, see) him since 2020.'
A: 'Since + point of time' in a negative sense takes the present perfect negative.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'We ___ (know) each other for many years.'
A: 'For + period' up to now takes the present perfect 'have known'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'While I ___ (walk) on the road, I met an old friend.'
A: 'While' introduces a longer background action, so the past continuous is used.

Q: Are the Tenses questions available in Assamese and English?
A: Yes — the content is fully bilingual. You can switch between Assamese and English at any point while working through Tenses, which helps when a term is clearer in one language than the other.
Q: Which exams is Tenses useful for?
A: Tenses is aligned with the ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC, Railway syllabus. The questions follow the pattern these papers use, so the practice carries over directly to the exam hall.
Q: What is tense in English grammar?
A: Tense is the form of a verb that shows the time of an action and whether it is finished, continuing or repeated.
Q: How many tenses are there in English?
A: There are twelve tenses, formed by combining three times (present, past and future) with four forms (simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous).
Q: What is the difference between the present perfect and the simple past?
A: The present perfect links a past action to the present and never takes a definite past time, while the simple past is used with a definite past time such as "yesterday".
Q: When do we use "since" and "for"?
A: "Since" is used with a point of time ("since 2019") and "for" with a period of time ("for three years"), usually in the perfect continuous.
Q: Which tense is used after "if" and "when"?
A: The present tense is used in the time or condition clause even when the meaning is about the future, as in "If it rains, we will stay".
Q: ইংৰাজী ব্যাকৰণত tense কাক বোলে?
A: Tense হৈছে ক্ৰিয়াৰ এনে ৰূপ যিয়ে কামটো কেতিয়া হৈছে আৰু সেয়া শেষ, চলি থকা নে পুনৰাবৃত্তি হোৱা দেখুৱায়।
Q: ইংৰাজীত কিমানটা tense আছে?
A: বাৰটা tense, যিবোৰ তিনিটা সময় (present, past, future) আৰু চাৰিটা ৰূপ (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) মিলি গঠন হয়।
Q: Present perfect আৰু simple past ৰ পাৰ্থক্য কি?
A: Present perfect এ অতীত কামক বৰ্তমানৰ লগত জুড়ি দিয়ে আৰু "yesterday" ধৰণৰ নিৰ্দিষ্ট অতীত সময় লোৱা নাই; simple past নিৰ্দিষ্ট অতীত সময়ৰ লগত ব্যৱহৃত হয়।
Q: "since" আৰু "for" কেতিয়া ব্যৱহাৰ হয়?
A: "since" সময়বিন্দুৰ লগত ("since 2019") আৰু "for" সময়কালৰ লগত ("for three years") ব্যৱহৃত হয়, সাধাৰণতে perfect continuous-ত।
Q: "if" আৰু "when" ৰ পিছত কোন tense ব্যৱহাৰ হয়?
A: অৰ্থ ভৱিষ্যতৰ হ'লেও সময় বা চৰ্তৰ খণ্ডবাক্যত present tense ব্যৱহাৰ হয়, যেনে "If it rains, we will stay"।

### Parts of Speech Questions with Answers — ADRE, APSC
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/english/parts-of-speech/
Summary: Practice parts of speech questions with step-by-step answers and explanations for ADRE, APSC and Assam Police. Free, bilingual, no sign-up.
Q: Which of these is a proper noun?
A: Brahmaputra is the name of a particular river, so it is a proper noun.
Q: Which word is a common noun?
A: A common noun names any person, place or thing of the same class. 'Table' is a common noun.
Q: Which of these is a collective noun?
A: A collective noun names a group. 'Crowd' means a group of people.
Q: Choose the correct collective noun: 'A ___ of cattle.'
A: A group of cattle is called a herd.
Q: Which of these is an abstract noun?
A: An abstract noun names a quality or idea. 'Kindness' cannot be seen or touched.
Q: 'Wisdom' is what kind of noun?
A: Wisdom is an idea or quality, so it is an abstract noun.
Q: Which of these is a material noun?
A: A material noun names a substance or material. 'Gold' is a material.
Q: Which of these is a countable noun?
A: 'Book' can be counted (one book, two books); the others are uncountable.
Q: Which of these is an uncountable noun?
A: 'Advice' is uncountable; we say 'some advice', not 'two advices'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The news ___ good.'
A: 'News' looks plural but is singular, so we use 'is'.
Q: Choose the correct plural of 'child'.
A: The plural of 'child' is 'children'.
Q: Choose the correct plural of 'ox'.
A: The plural of 'ox' is 'oxen'.
Q: Choose the correct plural of 'wife'.
A: Words ending in 'f'/'fe' often change to 'ves': wife → wives.
Q: Choose the correct plural of 'tooth'.
A: Irregular plural: tooth → teeth.
Q: The plural of 'sheep' is ___
A: 'Sheep' has the same form in singular and plural.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The scenery of Assam ___ beautiful.'
A: 'Scenery' is uncountable and singular, so we use 'is'.
Q: What is the feminine of 'actor'?
A: The feminine of 'actor' is 'actress'.
Q: What is the feminine of 'tiger'?
A: The feminine of 'tiger' is 'tigress'.
Q: The masculine of 'peahen' is ___
A: A male peafowl is a peacock; the female is a peahen.
Q: Which noun is of common gender?
A: 'Doctor' can refer to a male or a female, so it is common gender.
Q: Which noun is of neuter gender?
A: Neuter gender is used for lifeless things. 'Table' is a lifeless object.
Q: What is the noun form of the verb 'speak'?
A: The noun form of 'speak' is 'speech'. 'Speaker' is the person who speaks.
Q: Choose the correct collective noun: 'A ___ of ships.'
A: A group of ships is called a fleet.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The police ___ caught the thief.'
A: 'Police' is always used as a plural collective noun, so we use 'have'.
Q: Which word is a personal pronoun in 'She is my friend.'?
A: 'She' stands for a person and is a personal pronoun.
Q: 'I' is a pronoun of which person?
A: 'I' refers to the speaker, so it is first person.
Q: 'They' is a pronoun of which person?
A: 'They' refers to other people (not the speaker or listener), third person plural.
Q: Which is the possessive pronoun in 'This book is mine.'?
A: 'Mine' shows ownership and stands alone, so it is a possessive pronoun.
Q: Which word is an interrogative pronoun in 'Whose pen is this?'
A: 'Whose' asks a question and is an interrogative pronoun.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He hurt ___ while playing.'
A: When the subject and object are the same person, use a reflexive pronoun: himself.
Q: In 'I myself saw the accident', the word 'myself' is used as:
A: Here 'myself' gives emphasis to 'I', so it is an emphatic pronoun.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'They enjoyed ___ at the party.'
A: The correct reflexive form of 'they' is 'themselves'.
Q: Which demonstrative pronoun points to something near and singular?
A: 'This' points to a near, singular object.
Q: Which is the relative pronoun in 'The man who came is my uncle.'?
A: 'Who' connects the clause to 'the man' and is a relative pronoun.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This is the girl ___ won the prize.'
A: We use 'who' because it is the subject of 'won'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is the person ___ I met yesterday.'
A: 'Whom' is used as the object of the verb 'met'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Everyone must do ___ duty.'
A: 'Everyone' is singular, so the singular possessive 'his' is used in formal grammar.
Q: Which kind of pronoun is 'somebody' in 'Somebody has taken my pen.'?
A: 'Somebody' refers to an unknown person, so it is indefinite.
Q: Which kind of pronoun is 'each other' in 'They love each other.'?
A: 'Each other' shows a mutual action and is a reciprocal pronoun.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'None of the answers ___ correct.'
A: 'None' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'My brother and ___ went to the market.'
A: The subject needs the nominative case, so we use 'I'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Between you and ___, this plan will fail.'
A: After a preposition, we use the objective case 'me'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Neither of the boys ___ present.'
A: 'Neither' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the students ___ a book.'
A: 'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'has'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Let ___ go to the park.'
A: After 'let', we use the objective case 'him'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'It was ___ who called you.'
A: After 'was'/'is' the pronoun that follows the verb 'to be' takes the nominative form 'I' in formal grammar.
Q: A ship or a country is often referred to with which pronoun?
A: In literary English a ship or country is often referred to as 'she'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The committee members praised ___ for the success.'
A: The plural subject 'members' takes the plural reflexive 'themselves'.
Q: Identify the adjective in 'She is a beautiful girl.'
A: 'Beautiful' qualifies the noun 'girl' and is an adjective.
Q: In 'Give me some water', the word 'some' is an adjective of:
A: 'Some' shows how much water, so it is an adjective of quantity.
Q: In 'Two boys came', the word 'two' is an adjective of:
A: 'Two' shows how many, so it is an adjective of number.
Q: Which adjective in 'Each student got a prize' is distributive?
A: 'Each' distributes the idea to every single member of the group.
Q: Identify the demonstrative adjective in 'That book is mine.'
A: 'That' points out a particular book and modifies the noun 'book'.
Q: Which is the interrogative adjective in 'Which pen do you want?'
A: 'Which' asks a question and modifies the noun 'pen'.
Q: What type of adjective is 'my' in 'This is my house.'?
A: 'My' shows ownership and modifies the noun 'house', so it is a possessive adjective.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ than her sister.'
A: With 'than' we use the comparative degree 'taller'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Mount Everest is the ___ peak in the world.'
A: With 'the ... in the world' we use the superlative degree 'highest'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ taller than his brother.'
A: We use 'much' (not 'very') before a comparative adjective.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This is the ___ of the two books.'
A: When only two things are compared, we use the comparative 'better', not 'best'.
Q: What is the comparative degree of 'good'?
A: Irregular comparison: good → better → best.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is as ___ as his brother.'
A: In 'as ... as' we use the positive degree 'tall'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'There is ___ water in the glass.'
A: 'Water' is uncountable, so we use 'little', not 'few'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ people came to the meeting.' (meaning: almost nobody)
A: 'Few' (without 'a') means almost none, with a negative sense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I have ___ money than you.'
A: 'Money' is uncountable, so we use 'less', not 'fewer'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'My ___ brother is a doctor.' (referring to seniority)
A: 'Elder' is used for seniority among family members.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The ___ part of the book is more interesting.'
A: 'Latter' means the second of two things mentioned.
Q: Choose the correct order of adjectives: '___ saree'.
A: Order of adjectives: opinion before colour before material (beautiful → red → silk).
Q: Which word can be used as both an adjective and a noun?
A: 'Light' can be a noun (the light) or an adjective (a light bag). The others are fixed.
Q: Which sentence uses the adjective correctly?
A: We use either 'cleverer' or 'more clever', never both together.
Q: What is the superlative degree of 'little' (in quantity)?
A: For quantity: little → less → least.
Q: Which is the verb in 'He writes a letter.'?
A: 'Writes' shows the action done by the subject.
Q: In 'He kicked the ball', the verb 'kicked' is:
A: 'Kicked' takes an object 'the ball', so it is transitive.
Q: In 'The baby sleeps', the verb 'sleeps' is:
A: 'Sleeps' has no object, so it is intransitive.
Q: Identify the helping (auxiliary) verb in 'She is reading a book.'
A: 'Is' helps the main verb 'reading' to form the tense.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ___ swim very well.' (ability)
A: 'Can' expresses ability.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ I come in?' (asking permission)
A: 'May' is used for polite permission.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'You ___ not smoke in the hospital.' (prohibition)
A: 'Must not' expresses strong prohibition.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'We ___ respect our elders.' (duty)
A: 'Should' expresses duty or moral obligation.
Q: In 'I like to sing', the part 'to sing' is a/an:
A: 'To + verb' is an infinitive, a non-finite verb.
Q: In 'Swimming is good exercise', the word 'Swimming' is a:
A: A verb + ing used as a noun is a gerund. Here 'Swimming' is the subject.
Q: In 'The baby is sleeping', the word 'sleeping' is a:
A: Here 'sleeping' is used with 'is' to form the continuous tense, so it is a present participle.
Q: Choose the past participle of 'go'.
A: go → went (past) → gone (past participle).
Q: Choose the past tense of 'bring'.
A: The past tense of 'bring' is 'brought'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I ___ to school yesterday.'
A: With 'yesterday' we use the simple past 'went'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He has ___ his work.'
A: With 'has/have' we use the past participle 'done'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ (dance) now.'
A: In the present continuous tense we use 'is + verb-ing'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She has lived here ___ 2010.'
A: 'Since' is used before a point of time (2010); 'for' is used before a period.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the boys ___ done the homework.'
A: 'Each' is singular, so we use 'has'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The number of students ___ increasing.'
A: 'The number of' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'A number of students ___ absent today.'
A: 'A number of' is plural, so the verb is 'are'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The train ___ before I reached the station.'
A: For an action completed before another past action we use the past perfect 'had left'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I have ___ this film twice.'
A: 'Have + seen' (past participle) forms the present perfect.
Q: In 'I want to go home', which word is a finite verb?
A: 'Want' agrees with the subject and shows tense, so it is finite. 'To go' is non-finite.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She ___ to Guwahati next week.' (future plan)
A: For a future action we use 'will + verb'.
Q: Identify the adverb in 'She sings sweetly.'
A: 'Sweetly' tells how she sings and is an adverb of manner.
Q: 'Slowly' in 'The tortoise walks slowly' is an adverb of:
A: 'Slowly' shows the manner of walking.
Q: 'Tomorrow' in 'We will go tomorrow' is an adverb of:
A: 'Tomorrow' tells when the action happens, an adverb of time.
Q: 'Here' in 'Come here' is an adverb of:
A: 'Here' shows the place of the action.
Q: 'Always' in 'He always comes on time' is an adverb of:
A: 'Always' shows how often, an adverb of frequency.
Q: 'Very' in 'She is very beautiful' is an adverb of:
A: 'Very' shows the degree or intensity of 'beautiful'.
Q: Identify the adverb in 'The child is sleeping upstairs.'
A: 'Upstairs' shows where the child sleeps, an adverb of place.
Q: In 'The tea is too hot to drink', the adverb 'too' modifies:
A: 'Too' increases the degree of the adjective 'hot'.
Q: In 'She spoke quite clearly', the adverb 'quite' modifies:
A: 'Quite' modifies the adverb 'clearly'; an adverb can modify another adverb.
Q: Choose the adverb form of the adjective 'quick'.
A: Adding '-ly' to the adjective 'quick' gives the adverb 'quickly'.
Q: The sentence 'He hardly works' means:
A: 'Hardly' has a negative sense meaning 'almost not'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She writes ___ (neat).'
A: After the verb 'writes' we need an adverb, so 'neatly'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He ran ___ (fast) of all the boys.'
A: 'Fast' has the same form as adjective and adverb; its superlative is 'fastest'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She sings ___.' (good/well)
A: After an action verb we use the adverb 'well', not the adjective 'good'.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'He is a ___ player. He plays ___.'
A: After a noun we use the adjective 'good'; after a verb we use the adverb 'well'.
Q: Choose the correct sentence.
A: An adverb of frequency comes after the verb 'to be' ('is always late').
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I do not have ___ money.'
A: After the negative 'do not' we use 'any', not 'no' or 'some'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ enough to drive a car.'
A: 'Enough' comes after an adjective: 'old enough'.
Q: The sentence 'The box is too heavy to lift' means:
A: 'Too + adjective + to' means something cannot be done because of the extreme degree.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He speaks English ___ (fluent).'
A: The verb 'speaks' needs an adverb, so 'fluently'.
Q: Choose the adverb of frequency from the options.
A: 'Often' tells how frequently. 'Here' (place), 'now' (time), 'very' (degree).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is good ___ English.'
A: We say 'good at' a subject or skill.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is afraid ___ dogs.'
A: We say 'afraid of' something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I am proud ___ my country.'
A: We say 'proud of' someone or something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'This book consists ___ ten chapters.'
A: We say 'consist of' meaning 'to be made up of'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He insisted ___ going there.'
A: We say 'insist on' doing something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is married ___ a doctor.'
A: We say 'married to' someone.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He died ___ fever.'
A: We die 'of' a disease but 'from' a wound or injury.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The train arrived ___ time.'
A: 'On time' means at the correct time, not late.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She has been waiting ___ two hours.'
A: 'For' is used before a period of time like 'two hours'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'We reached the station ___ time to catch the train.'
A: 'In time' means early enough to do something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He jumped ___ the river.'
A: 'Into' shows movement from outside to the inside of something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The cat is ___ the table.'
A: 'On' means resting on the surface of the table.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I am going ___ Delhi tomorrow.'
A: We use 'to' before a place we travel towards.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He lives ___ Guwahati.'
A: We use 'in' before the names of cities and towns.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'We sleep ___ night.'
A: We say 'at night' and 'in the morning'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The classes start ___ 9 o'clock.'
A: We use 'at' before exact clock time.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He was born ___ Sunday morning.'
A: We use 'on' before a particular day with part of the day.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The thief entered ___ the window.'
A: 'Through' shows passing from one side to the other inside something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He sat ___ two friends.'
A: 'Between' is used for two persons or things; 'among' for more than two.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'The meeting is ___ Monday.'
A: We use 'on' before the days of the week.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I agree ___ you on this point.'
A: We 'agree with' a person but 'agree to' a proposal.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Success depends ___ hard work.'
A: We say 'depend on' something.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She congratulated me ___ my success.'
A: We say 'congratulate someone on something'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is good ___ solving puzzles.'
A: We use 'good at' + gerund (doing something).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is poor ___ honest.'
A: 'But' shows contrast between 'poor' and 'honest'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I like tea ___ coffee.'
A: 'And' joins two similar ideas.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Hurry up, ___ you will miss the bus.'
A: 'Or' shows the result or alternative: otherwise you will miss the bus.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I waited ___ he came back.'
A: 'Until' means up to the time that he came back.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He did not come ___ he was ill.'
A: 'Because' gives the reason for not coming.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'You can take ___ tea ___ coffee.'
A: 'Either ... or' shows a choice between two things.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'He is ___ rich ___ happy.'
A: 'Neither ... nor' negates both: not rich and not happy.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ he is rich, he is not happy.'
A: 'Though' shows contrast: in spite of being rich, he is unhappy.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'He is ___ weak ___ he cannot walk.'
A: 'So ... that' (with a clause) shows result. Note: 'too ... to' is followed by a verb, not a clause.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'She is ___ beautiful ___ intelligent.'
A: 'Not only ... but also' joins two positive qualities of equal importance.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ he saw me, he ran away.'
A: 'As soon as' means immediately when.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'You will fail ___ you work hard.'
A: 'Unless' means 'if not': you will fail if you do not work hard.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Work hard ___ you should fail.'
A: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and is followed by 'should'.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'He is ___ a doctor ___ a teacher.'
A: 'Both ... and' shows he has two roles at the same time.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Scarcely had he left ___ it began to rain.'
A: 'Scarcely' is paired with 'when'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'No sooner had I reached ___ the train left.'
A: 'No sooner' is paired with 'than'.
Q: Which of these is a subordinating conjunction?
A: 'Although' joins a dependent clause to the main clause. 'But, and, or' are coordinating.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I will not go ___ you come with me.'
A: 'Unless' = if not. I will go only if you come with me.
Q: Identify the interjection in 'Hurrah! We have won the match.'
A: 'Hurrah!' expresses sudden joy and is an interjection.
Q: In 'Alas! He is no more', the word 'Alas' expresses:
A: 'Alas!' is used to express sorrow or grief.
Q: Which interjection expresses sudden joy?
A: 'Hurrah!' is used to show joy.
Q: In 'Hush! The baby is sleeping', 'Hush' means:
A: 'Hush!' tells people to be silent.
Q: In 'Bravo! You have played well', 'Bravo' is used to express:
A: 'Bravo!' expresses admiration or praise.
Q: Which part of speech expresses sudden emotion or feeling?
A: An interjection is a word that expresses sudden feeling, e.g., Oh!, Alas!, Hurrah!.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___! I have lost my purse.'
A: Losing a purse brings grief, so 'Alas!' fits.
Q: Identify the interjection in 'Oh! What a beautiful sight it is.'
A: 'Oh!' stands alone to express wonder or surprise.
Q: In 'Fie! You told a lie', the word 'Fie' expresses:
A: 'Fie!' expresses disgust or disapproval.
Q: Which word is an interjection in 'Aha! I found my key.'?
A: 'Aha!' expresses sudden satisfaction or discovery.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ engineer.'
A: 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound, so we use 'an'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ honest man.'
A: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound ('h' is silent), so we use 'an'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He studies at ___ university.'
A: 'University' starts with the consonant sound 'yoo', so we use 'a'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He came ___ hour ago.'
A: 'Hour' begins with a vowel sound ('h' is silent), so we use 'an'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ sun rises in the east.'
A: 'The' is used before unique things like the sun, the moon, the earth.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ Ganga is a holy river.'
A: 'The' is used before the names of rivers.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'The rich should help ___ poor.'
A: 'The + adjective' (the poor, the rich) refers to a whole class of people.
Q: Choose the correct option for the sentence: '___ Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.'
A: Before 'Mount + name' we do not use any article.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ best singer in the class.'
A: 'The' is used before a superlative degree.
Q: Fill in the blanks: 'I have ___ apple and ___ banana.'
A: 'Apple' has a vowel sound (an), 'banana' has a consonant sound (a).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'Please carry ___ umbrella.'
A: 'Umbrella' begins with the vowel sound 'u', so we use 'an'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'He is ___ MLA.'
A: Abbreviations said as letters (M-L-A) start with a vowel sound 'em', so 'an MLA'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I saw ___ one-eyed man on the road.'
A: 'One' begins with the consonant sound 'w', so we use 'a one-eyed'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'I need ___ milk to make tea.'
A: 'Some' is used before uncountable nouns like milk.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'How ___ time do you need?'
A: 'Time' is uncountable, so we use 'much'.
Q: Fill in the blank: 'How ___ books are there on the shelf?'
A: 'Books' is countable, so we use 'many'.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ of the two answers is correct.'
A: 'Neither' is used for two; 'none/no one' are used for more than two.
Q: Which determiner means 'some (positive amount)' with uncountable nouns?
A: 'A little' means some (positive), while 'little' means hardly any (negative).
Q: Fill in the blank: 'You may take ___ of the two books.'
A: 'Either' means one of the two.
Q: Fill in the blank: '___ of the students was given a prize.'
A: 'Each' can stand alone before 'of', but 'every' cannot be used with 'of'.
Q: In 'He runs fast', the word 'fast' is a/an:
A: 'Fast' tells how he runs, so it is an adverb.
Q: In 'He is a fast bowler', the word 'fast' is a/an:
A: 'Fast' qualifies the noun 'bowler', so it is an adjective.
Q: In 'I walk to school every day', the word 'walk' is a/an:
A: Here 'walk' shows the action of the subject, so it is a verb.
Q: In 'He took a walk in the park', the word 'walk' is a/an:
A: Here 'walk' is the object of 'took' and names a thing, so it is a noun.
Q: In 'Please water the plants', the word 'water' is a/an:
A: Here 'water' means to pour water on, so it is a verb.
Q: In 'Drink a glass of water', the word 'water' is a/an:
A: Here 'water' names a substance, so it is a noun (material noun).
Q: In 'She has a sweet voice', the word 'sweet' is a/an:
A: 'Sweet' qualifies the noun 'voice', so it is an adjective.
Q: In 'He answered all the questions', the word 'answered' is a/an:
A: 'Answered' shows the action, so it is a verb.
Q: In 'Her answer was correct', the word 'answer' is a/an:
A: Here 'answer' is the subject of the sentence, so it is a noun.
Q: In 'He cut the wood with a saw', the word 'saw' is a/an:
A: Here 'saw' names a tool, so it is a noun.
Q: In 'I saw a tiger in the forest', the word 'saw' is a/an:
A: Here 'saw' is the past tense of 'see', showing an action.
Q: In 'Please turn the light on', the word 'on' is a/an:
A: Here 'on' is joined to the verb 'turn' with no object after it, so it is an adverb.
Q: In 'The book is on the table', the word 'on' is a/an:
A: Here 'on' relates the noun 'table' to 'book', so it is a preposition.
Q: In 'Please book a ticket for me', the word 'book' is a/an:
A: Here 'book' means to reserve, so it is a verb.
Q: In 'This book is very interesting', the word 'book' is a/an:
A: Here 'book' is a thing, the subject of the sentence, so it is a noun.
Q: In 'She has a beautiful smile', the word 'smile' is a/an:
A: Here 'smile' is the object of 'has', so it is a noun.
Q: In 'He smiled at me', the word 'smiled' is a/an:
A: 'Smiled' shows the action, so it is a verb.
Q: In 'They live near the river', the word 'near' is a/an:
A: Here 'near' shows the relation with the noun 'river', so it is a preposition.
Q: In 'The final exam is near', the word 'near' is a/an:
A: Here 'near' describes the subject 'exam', so it is an adjective (predicative use).
Q: In 'Please open the window', the word 'open' is a/an:
A: Here 'open' shows an action done to the window, so it is a verb.
Q: In 'The window is open', the word 'open' is a/an:
A: Here 'open' describes the state of the window, so it is an adjective.
Q: In 'She works in a bank', the word 'bank' is a/an:
A: Here 'bank' names a place, so it is a noun.
Q: In 'She sings well', the word 'well' is a/an:
A: 'Well' tells how she sings, so it is an adverb of manner.
Q: In 'He is not well today', the word 'well' is a/an:
A: After 'is' (linking verb) 'well' means healthy and is an adjective.
